newsitem.title: UK: Debt markets set to sprint ahead on U.S. election.
newsitem.headline: Debt markets set to sprint ahead on U.S. election.

text.p: By Jacqueline Thorpe,
Global debt markets were set to charge ahead on Wednesday, spurred on by a strong Treasuries market as U.S. presidential elections maintained the status quo in U.S. politics, analysts said.
The elections gave bond markets the best they could have hoped for -- a Democrat in the White House but Republicans still in control, they said.

"The fact that we're not getting a major fiscal risk in the U.S. is good for all bond markets," said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in London. "Inevitably Europe will be dragged higher by the sharp rally we've seen overnight," he said.

Stephen Hannah, head of research at IBJ International in London, added, "On the U.S. side, if the market can fall below 6.5 percent on the long bond it may make a stab at six percent and that will pull up the other markets."
"That's a fairly important barrier but I don't sense at the moment investors are likely to weigh in with heavy profit taking," he said.

Some profit-taking had taken the shine off early Treasury gains, traders said, with the bellwether long bond slipping to to 101-29 by 1408 GMT from the 102-04 finish in New York on Tuesday. The yield was at 6.602 percent.
Earlier, the yield dipped to 6.56 percent, its lowest level since the March 7 close -- the day before a jump in U.S. payrolls sent international debt markets into a tailspin.
December T-bond futures were quoted at 113-20, down 5/32 on the day.

In Europe, December Bund futures on LIFFE were quoted at 100.20, up eight basis points from Tuesday. French bond futures were also up but other markets fell back after sharp gains earlier in the day. British gilts were down 7/32 at 109-03.

The elections put Democratic President Bill Clinton firmly back in the White House as he routed Republican Bob Dole in a re-election sweep but the Republicans maintained control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives.

Chester said there may be some profit taking with the election result widely expected but Hannah at IBJ noted the wall of Japanese money that has been supporting bond markets is not likely to disappear any time soon.

"There is no shortage of global liquidity," Hannah said. "The Japanese monetary system is still in a delicate position which requires the Bank of Japan to maintain record low interest rates and that -- through capital outflows -- is fuelling continued upward presssure on bond prices all over the globe."
Analysts said key for debt markets was Republican control of Congress which would put a curb on Democratic policies that markets generally perceive to favour spending.
"With the Republicans maintaining control of the Congress nobody really expects the budget deficit to widen too dramatically over the next couple of years," Hannah said.
While U.S. Treasuries were well-supported to move ahead, European markets would now focus on other issues, namely European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), analysts said.

Hannah said this would likely lead core European debt to lag Treasuries. Bunds, and bonds linked closely to the German market like Austrian and French debt, would suffer while Italian, Spanish and other high yielding debt would gain, he said.

Stuart Thomson, chief international economist at Nikko Europe here, agreed, saying the next meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on November 13 was likely to be a non-event as markets expect interest rates to stay steady.

He said Greenspan has achieved a "soft-landing" in the economy. While it was reasonable to expect a buoyant Christmas sales period as a result of higher earnings in the U.S., data show spenders have been restrained so far.
"In essence what the electorate have voted for is Greenspan and his exceptional record which has placed Clinton in a position of power," he said.
